query_text: how do bacteriophages differ from antibiotics

content.text:
Bacteriophages (“phages”) and antibiotics both can kill bacteria, but they work very differently.

| Feature | Bacteriophages | Antibiotics |
|---|---|---|
| **What they are** | Viruses that infect bacteria | Chemical drugs, natural or synthetic |
| **Target specificity** | Usually very specific: often infect only certain bacterial species or strains | Often broader: may affect many types of bacteria |
| **How they kill bacteria** | Attach to a bacterium, inject genetic material, replicate inside it, and often burst it open | Interfere with bacterial processes like cell-wall synthesis, protein production, DNA replication, or metabolism |
| **Effect on microbiome** | May spare most “good” bacteria because of narrow targeting | Can disrupt normal gut/skin bacteria, especially broad-spectrum antibiotics |
| **Resistance** | Bacteria can become resistant to phages, but phages can also evolve in response | Bacteria can become resistant to antibiotics; antibiotic resistance is a major global problem |
| **Use in medicine** | Used in some places and studied for difficult resistant infections; often customized to the bacterial strain | Widely used standard treatment for bacterial infections |
| **Self-amplification** | Can multiply at the infection site if matching bacteria are present | Do not replicate; drug levels depend on dosing and metabolism |
| **Limitations** | Need the right phage for the exact bacteria; immune system may neutralize them; regulatory/standardization challenges | Side effects, allergies, resistance, and damage to beneficial bacteria |

**In short:** antibiotics are chemical treatments that often act broadly against bacteria, while bacteriophages are bacteria-infecting viruses that tend to be highly targeted. Phages may be especially useful against antibiotic-resistant infections, but they usually require careful matching to the infecting bacterial strain.
